utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, the 21st of February, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution, to Mr. Seselj, to the witness, and to all those assisting us in and around this courtroom. Today, we'll proceed with the examination-in-chief of the witness. Let's hope that we can complete it today for us to then be able to start cross-examination. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to do one more War Staff document picking up on where we were yesterday and then move on to another topic. The issue we were at yesterday was the issue of assistance to the TOs for assistance by various organisations for assistance from the War Staff. And if Your Honours would look in binder 1, I'd like to take you to Exhibit number 1555, which will be the seventh tab in binder 1 if you count them down. Actually, did I say binder 1, because that is incorrect. It's binder 2. The document is on the screen. I guess old habits die hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we have -- we have seen and talked about requests from various TOs for assistance from the War Staff. Now, this document, could you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a request from the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 327th Brigade for manpower -- to provide manpower by the SRS War Staff. Looking at the contents of the document, one can conclude that the 327th Brigade is a unit of the VRS, and that means also the 2nd Motorised Battalion is a unit of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we haven't come to this yet, but the VRS, as I understand your report, was the successor, so to speak, of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We will cover this later.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The VRS was established in the course of the decision to establish the VRS was taken in May 1992. The VRS relied largely on the manpower and equipment of the JNA 2nd Military District, as well as on manpower of the local Serb TO which had been established in the meanwhile in Serb-controlled or Serb-held parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this will be addressed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The only reason I bring this up here, and this is the last document on the structure of the VRS, was to illustrate that there were also requests for assistance to the War Staff from other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a technical military-type question to ask you. This document has been issued by Captain 1st Class Slavko Crnic, the commander, who apparently is a member of a 327th Brigade, which is, in it's turn, part of the 2nd Motorised Battalion. The VRS is either de facto or de jure an army, because at the time the Republika Srpska proclaimed itself as such. This request for additional manpower, shouldn't it have gone through its own chain of command, the chain of command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a correct observation. From this one document, we cannot establish whether or not this battalion commander first directed such a request through the chain of command. It's still quite early, so we're August 1992. The VRS is in full development. I have included in the report, in the section Bosnia and Herzegovina, an assessment by General Mladic where he says that in certain parts of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the integration of local Serb TO units, as well as of other armed units, into the VRS is moving on slowing, which could also then indicate that this has also an effect on the functions of the chain of command in those areas. I remember from other documents on logistical support, so requests from Bosnian Serb units to Serbia or SFRY for logistical support which are not included in my report here, that there, too, there were direct requests from battalion or brigade commanders to units of the VJ or commands in the VJ; and in response, orders were issued both within the VJ as well within the VRS and also in Croatia in the SVK where similar problems arose. So orders were issued to prevent lower-level commanders from making direct requests and actually circumventing the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'd like to tender Exhibit 1555 at this stage, and that does not have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 242.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now going to move to the bigger picture and discuss with the witness the -- his conclusions with respect to the situation in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have reviewed the questions Your Honours have been having over the last days to the witness about some of the very specific issues we have been discussing, and I appreciate there's the difficulty in that we have not had some of the insider witnesses who can also speak to these points that were foreseen to come before this witness. So I fully appreciate the difficulties in grasping at this stage some of the issues; and, hopefully, the reverse order of the witnesses mean that we can clarify some of these issues later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But I'd like to some up, Mr. Theunens, just some of your conclusions with respect to the SRS and its interactions with the JNA and the local TOs. The issues we have discussed, and I know you have already tried to cover this, but in very simple terms, first of all, in your view, did the SRS have a military-type structure?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the SRS, as such, as a political party had no military-type structure as far as I'm aware. However, they established a body known as the SRS War Staff which, based on the documents I reviewed, carried out duties that included the recruitment, facilitating of the training, the equipment or the facilitating of the equipment, as well as the dispatching and the payment or the facilitating of the payment of volunteers to various conflict areas in Croatia. When these volunteers who were then operating in their distinct detachments or formations were in the conflict area, they maintained relations with the SRS War Staff. There was, for example, there were exchanges of operational information. Members of the SRS War Staff were sent to the area where the SRS volunteer detachment was active to inspect the -- the situation with the volunteers and, if necessary, issue orders to improve the situation. There were also promotions carried out by the SRS of SRS volunteers who were considered meritorious, which brings me to the last point that the SRS volunteer detachment operating in the field had a military structure and functioned along military lines. And to be entirely correct, and I apologise for being so extensive, the documents that I reviewed in relation to the role of these volunteers in the conflict show that most of the times, and in particular most of the times after September 1991, these volunteers in the conflict in Croatia, so these SRS volunteers, operate under the command and control of the JNA. Prior to September 1991, the documents indicate that VRS volunteers operate in -- in their own structure in certain areas, and there are no indication that this is happening under the command of the JNA. The situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is more complicated, and I think it's better to address that once we are going into the details of the various locations discussed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Theunens, just to make one point clear, have you seen any operational or combat orders issued by the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I've only seen -- I mean, the closest reference I have seen are comments made by SRS volunteers. For example, in articles that were published in the SRS party magazine, Velika Srbija, whereby these volunteers state they have been sent or they have been deployed with their detachment upon the order of the SRS War Staff or Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your view, could SRS volunteers have been deployed on the ground in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina without the support of other -- without the support of state structures, either federal or Republican?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and it's not only a matter of support, i.e., logistical aspects that these people have to be equipped. They need to have a weapon. They need ammunition. They need uniforms. But it's also a matter of authorisation. As I mentioned before, in an area where military or combat operations are conducted, there is a commander who is responsible for that situation in the area, which means that he also determines and decides which forces will operate in that area. So, if SRS volunteers are operating in an area where there is a JNA unit and the JNA unit is conducting operations, there needs to have been given an authorisation by the most senior JNA officer in the area. From the documents I have reviewed, I can conclude -- conclude that it -- that this authorisation was not just issued on the local level but that was part of a policy which had been decided upon at the highest level. See, for example, the various decrees and orders we discussed from the political leadership to legalise and regularise the participation of volunteers, including volunteer formations in the conflict in Croatia during fall and winter 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope this sort of recap of the evidence is helpful, and I now move to the specific -- more specific situation on the ground in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, you and your colleagues must see clearly that this is a change to the expert report, because this observation is not contained in the expert report, and it goes along the lines of my objections. I am happy to hear it, but we can't say that it's recapitulation when it is in fact an amendment to the expert report, especially the part up to September 1991 and after September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm happy to re-qualify my qualification of what it is the witness have just done and say I hope this testimony by the witness is helpful to the court. The witness is obviously at liberty to give his conclusions to before Chamber. That's why he's here. So I don't think there's any basis for the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness is giving us his findings. And, Mr. Seselj, during the cross-examination, you will be able to fight him with your questions and then we will make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, for background, could you please describe the military situation in February, March 1991, in Croatia for us.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not discussed that topic in detail in my report, so I will -- may mention now certain things which are not included in the report. What one can say is that overall the situation in Croatia and also Slovenia is tense, because from the political level, there are movements for independence, sometimes qualified as secession by others, by Slovenia and Croatia. At the same, time we know, for example, that in areas with a significant Serb presence in Croatia, mainly the area known as Krajina, as well, and that is at later stage Eastern Slavonia, local Serbs feel -- are worried about the situation. At the same moment, we can see that on both -- on both sides, Croatia as well as Serbia, there is increased use of the media in order to, and that is my conclusion, increase actually ethnic tensions and even ethnic fears among the main ethnic groups that are involved in the situation; namely, the Serbs, and I mean by that Serbs in Croatia, as well as the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard you well; and while I was listening to what you were saying, I was looking at Annex 1 of the indictment, which is outlining the additional events, you know, as to what happened in Croatia; and in March 1991, it is said that there are conflicts in Pakrac and so on. On April 1st, the Executive Council of the Krajina SAO passed a resolution so that it could be attached to the Republic of Serbia. So it looks like in March and April there is actually great agitation, and some are calling for an attachment to Serbia; but legally Croatia, it doesn't exist yet. We're still in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So, in this kind of situation, the JNA, which is the legal army, armed force, what exactly is its position, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the JNA is in a difficult position, because when you look at the constitutional mission of the JNA, the JNA has the mission to safeguard the territorial integrity, the independence, the sovereignty, and the social order within the SFRY. We see from the events in -- for this happening in January and March that the SSNO, so the Federal Secretary for People's Detection, Kadijevic, in January and March 1991, tries to convince the SFRY Presidency, which is the Supreme Command, to decide on the establishment of the state of emergency, in order to allow the armed forces to restore order. Because of the incidents you mentioned, Pakrac, there's also Plitvice, there's later Glina, they are related to similar -- to a similar situation, even though the development of each individual incident is slightly different. Basically, Croatia tries to establish Croatian police stations in a number of areas; I mean by that police stations which are manned predominantly by Croats. From the information I have reviewed - it is not included in the report but in the framework of my previous work - the conclusion can be drawn that the police in Croatia, there is a significant presence of Serbs in that -- in the national police of the Republic of Croatia, in particular in areas with a significant Serb presence, which, from a common sense point of view, makes sense. Now, in a situation where Croatia is striving for independence, one of the first things they try to do is to establish their authority. In August 1990, so more than half a year before, we have the Log or the Balvan Revolution in Knin where local Serbs, according to some sources assisted by Serbs from outside of Croatia, establish barricades and prevent, for example, the -- the use of Croatian symbols or use of Croatian shields, I mean, on police stations in Pakrac and Plitvice. In Pakrac, from the information I consulted, the situation is that Serbs have occupied local municipal offices as well as the police office, and Croatia then sends -- or the Croatian authorities send special policemen from Zagreb in order to establish or restore Croatian authority over the police station in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer, but this is my problem: When I read, you know, the submissions of the accusation of Prosecution, you know, this of course is in support of the Prosecution's case, which is normal; but as a Judge, you know, I must try to be on another level. In what the -- in the report of the Prosecution that we have in Appendix 1, it seems that everything comes from nationalists, from the nationalist political parties; whereas, one could wonder on the Croatian side, you know, who -- who is pushing for independence and recognition, and this is missing in the indictment. It's really not mentioned in Annex, 1; and because of this, a question comes to my mind, and you're giving me a good opportunity to put this question. You're telling me that Croats wanted to take control of the police stations and so on. If Croats are doing something, it's probably that they have intentions, and then Serbs from Croatia probably know that the JNA is not doing anything because of the constitutional order's, the order of the SFRY. But, obviously, they see that the JNA is not intervening; and given the threat that's looming ahead of -- on their head, you know, they maybe decide to go to self-defence, prepare their own self-defence, and maybe call on help in Serbia to help get people to help them, which is how we could end up with volunteers. So, according to you, is this possible? Is this a possible scenario?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not -- I want to emphasise that I have not studied or analysed the -- the particularities of the developments in March -- between March and, say, June 1991 in Croatia. What I'm explaining now is based on my understanding of the conflict following the work I have done and the studies I have -- I have conducted outside the framework of this report. It is obvious that even before Croatia tries to establish authority over police stations located on its territory, i.e., within its -- which should be within it's control, there is already tension and the spirits have been heated up as a consequence of not only media reports but also statements on all sides, statements by senior politicians on all sides. Coming myself from a country which could not be considered multi-ethnic but at least there are several communities with different languages who sometimes have difficulties to understand each other, I realise the seriousness or the importance of the effects the media can have on the attitude of the average population, in particular taking into account the history of the area. The memories of the Second World War and what the NDH did to Serbs and so on is very fresh with people, especially in areas like the Krajina. Now, all these fears and all these tensions are actually not only reawakened but are intensified by the media, state-controlled media on both sides, in the course of 1990 and 1991, even earlier. After the death of Tito in 1980, we slowly see a development in SFRY whereby people or some people address nationalistic issues. Sometimes they're put in prison, but they go much further than they would ever have dared to do when Tito was still alive, when all these issues were basically forbidden to be -- it was not allowed to address these issues in public and where, for example, the JNA and other federal institutions were all promoting the slogan of "Brotherhood and Unity," brotherhood and unity between all nationalities and the people of SFRY. What we see is -- okay. We have both sides ethnic tensions increasing. We also see that both sides are organising and arming themselves. And I'm not in a position here to provide details on who started first and who did what at which location. But, again, based on my recollection, I can say that it's happening on -- on the two sides. I think the Balvan Revolution in August 1990, so the -- excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We already understand all this. This is very interesting, but you're talking about two sides. I'd like to know if you agree with the fact -- with the following fact: If I'm not wrong, up until January 1992, when Slovenia and Croatia were recognised by the European Community, up until then Yugoslavia still existed with its international borders as they were; Yugoslavia as member of the EC, with its borders as it were. So, up until January 1992, in terms of international law, they were not -- there were not two sides. You can't talk about two sides. Do you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not a constitutional expert, so I would prefer not to express myself on -- on such a legal issue. I can only mention some factual issues; that is, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But am I right or wrong? Isn't it in January 1992 that the international community recognised these countries and that there was the first disintegration, if I could say so, of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do remember that, and it happened in -- it didn't happen all at the same time. But already end of December or early January 1992, I think Germany recognised Croatia, and then the other EC member countries followed. But if you allow me, I would -- and not to show or to create an impression that I disagree with you, not at all, but just from the factual point of view, in July -- on the 8th and the 9th of July, 1991, there is the -- a peace conference in Brioni sponsored by the -- or supervised by the EC, where one of the four points of the declaration is that Slovenia and Croatia postpone their declaration of independence with three months. So instead of the 26th -- or 25th and 26th of June, it is postponed to October 1991, and that is all I can say about this. What the legal implications are of the Brioni Declaration in relation to the recognition by the EC as you pointed out in January 1992, I don't think that's something which is up to me to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, to follow up on my fellow Judge's question. It's important to note at this juncture that until January 1992, the former Yugoslavia still exists with its international borders as recognised by the international community. Of course, your report is a military report. It's a military analysis; and, therefore, the question that springs to our mind and springs to everyone's mind is the following: Given all the events that are occurring on the field in 1991, what exactly is the position of the JNA? The JNA is supposed to be the striking force of the SFRY, of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So could you confirm that at the time the general heading the JNA was General Kadijevic? Was he the general heading the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. General Kadijevic is the chief of the staff of the Supreme Command; and, as such, he's the most senior military person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then using all the documents you have you've seen on the JNA, have you tried to find out what was the position of these generals, including Kadijevic? Remember that he is mentioned in the indictment as being part of JCE, and maybe the Trial Chamber would want to hear him as a court witness if he's not called by Prosecution or by the accused. So, in the framework your report, did you try and understand what was the exact position of the JNA and, of course, its number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may just assist the -- Your Honours with a reference on this, because this was exactly thing I was going to move into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe this is being discussed in part 2, part 2 of the expert report beginning at page 7, and that's page 107 in the B/C/S version, where there is a discussion about the change of the mission during the conflict in Croatia. I believe Judge Harhoff, at page 3719 Thursday last week, also approached this topic a bit, or the expert approached this document in answer to a question by Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you have explained us what the constitutional mission of the JNA was. Was there, based on your analysis, a change in the constitutional mission during the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Indeed, there was a change in the mission of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When was that change?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will refer to what General Kadijevic wrote in this his book, "My View of the Break-up." He gives a rather -- a very analytical view in the is sense that he distinguishes two phases in the conflict in Croatia, a first phase which is called by him -- or determined by him as starting mid-March with what he calls the first attacks on Serbs in the Krajina until the end of summer. That's the first phase according to Kadijevic. Then Kadijevic sees a second phase from the end of summer until the acceptance of the Vance Plan, which is end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And before -- before we go into the details of this, could you just summarise what was the change in the mission?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the change in the mission, according to Kadijevic and orders from Adzic and Kadijevic, is that instead of maintaining the -- or pursuing the constitutional mission including maintaining the territorial integrity, the mission then for what Croatia is concerned is changed into interposition between the armed factions. Then the third development is that the mission is changed into what is called protecting the Serbs, and what is called by Kadijevic as liberating the Serb areas in Croatia, assisting the Krajina Serbs in organising their own armed forces, and withdrawing the JNA garrisons and barracks from Croatia, i.e., those garrisons and barracks located outside the areas under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You were extremely fast. But if I understood you well, there was a change in position. First, the JNA interfered, interposed itself between the two factions, if I could say so, the two sides. That's the first thing. Then the second change in the mission is that they decided to protect the Serbs. Then the third one possibly was the withdrawal. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The examples you mentioned, like Pakrac and Plitvice, there the JNA intervenes to officially to interpose itself between the armed -- between the two sides. The Serbs say, well, this is to protect ourselves. The Croats are unhappy because they say actually the JNA -- the JNA is now consolidating Serb control over Croatian territory. Something similar happens in Borovo Selo in May, early May 1992. Then, over summer, the goal changes into what is officially called protecting the Serbs, but that is the way how the JNA represents it. The Croats say, well, actually, the JNA is consolidating Serb control over parts of Croatia and actually expanding that control to all areas that are considered Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So were these changes made by the Presidency of the Federal Republic or behind the backs of the Presidency? Were these carried out by the military who decided this of their own accord, that they decided to operate these changes which we could perhaps qualify or term constitutional changes? According to you, this was done with the approval of the Presidency or against the approval of the Presidency because this does have consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is clear that initially, and I'm speaking now about spring 1991, the JNA or Kadijevic is seeking instructions from the Presidency; and, for example, the minutes of the Presidency session of -- I think it's 12th of March, 1991, are quite interesting in that context. They are not addressed in my report. But later on we see that actually a third option applies. That is from the book by Jovic, Borisav Jovic, who is, in June 1991, the outgoing chairman of the SFRY Presidency. We see that Kadijevic and Adzic are getting their instructions not from the SFRY Presidency but from certain members of the Presidency, as well as from people who are not members of the Presidency. And if I remember well, this was addressed last week where -- where we, for example, discussed this chart, showing that there were 27 meetings between Jovic and Kadijevic during, say, August to December 1991 time period, and whereby actually Mesic was the official chairman of the Presidency. Jovic was the outgoing chairman. He was not even the acting chairman because that was Kostic. And, also, Slobodan Milosevic, the President of Serbia, who is not part of the Supreme Command, became involved in giving instructions to Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may interject here, this was discussed at pages 3694 and 3695 of the transcript where there was a discussion of the July meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Theunens, now that we're on the topic of the meeting, you testified and you have mentioned at page 6 in your report, that's pages 106 and 107 of the B/C/S version, that Milosevic and Jovic instructed Kadijevic to concentrate forces along certain axes or certain areas, and that Kadijevic accepted this. Now, I wonder if I could ask you to draw - I know these are very general areas - but if you could maybe draw on this map for us...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I could gets the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: ... the areas that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could place this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Jovic in his book says Milosevic and Kadijevic asked him to concentrate the main forces of the JNA along a line which goes in the west from Karlovac to Plitvice, whereby Karlovac is located here. Plitvice falls are located more or less there. That's the western limit. The eastern limit would be Baranja, Vinkovci. Then in the south, he talks about the Neretva River or he mentioned the Neretva River which runs more or less there. Now, this is a bit abstract. But when we look at -- we consider a map with the ethnic distribution, as it was established in 1991 based on the results of the census in 1991, we see that the areas in Croatia with the main -- where the Serbs are more or less concentrated are indeed located more or less this way, especially in -- I mean, in particular in the municipality of Knin as well as Glina, the Serbs have a majority according to the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I am just going to stop you because later on, when the transcript is looked at, it's going to be difficult to relate this to the actual exhibit. Now, you drew a number of, just now, a number of dotted lines, and I believe within those lines there is the Serb -- the concentration of Serb population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then the first line you described, the Karlovac-Plitvice line, could you put an "A" where that line is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you put a "B" at the eastern line.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] These are the western limits. "A" is the western limit. "B" is the eastern limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And down south along the river, if you'd put a "C"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P243.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. President. Is this map an exhibit, what the witness has been drawing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I ask that a copy be given to me also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You will get a copy of this. Would you kindly make a copy for Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj interrupted me just at the time I wanted to put you a question, Witness. You have positioned the JNA in three areas, sector A, sector B. You say, if I've understood you correctly, that the troops were positioned there because there is a high concentration of Serbs, is that right, and they are predominantly Serb in that area, and that is why the JNA was concentrated there? Is that in military terms what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is what Jovic says in his book. He says that by deploying or concentrating the main forces of the JNA between western limit, the line Karlovac-Plitvice; eastern limit, Baranja, Osijek, Vinkovci; and towards the Sava, which I didn't mark on the map but it's the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; and the south in Neretva, the JNA is concentrated in the areas -- excuse me, the JNA would cover all Serb populated territory, I'm quoting from Jovic, "until the situation is fully resolved, i.e., until a final expression of popular will in a referendum." That is what Jovic writes in his published diary for the 5th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Seselj will be given a copy of this straight away. The registrar has just told me that he will give you a copy of this map during the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, just to try to tie the different pieces together before we continue with these different phases, during this period that we just discussed, were there also -- were there deployment of SRS volunteers in some of these same areas?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. As is discussed in the section on Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as early as April 1991, SRS volunteers are being sent to certain parts of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We've already covered this and we're going to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just as a point, Your Honours, at page 10, and that's page 111 of the B/C/S, there is a map which illustrates I believe what the plan was for the first phase -- no, sorry. The second stage of the first -- the first stage of the second phase of the developments in Croatia. Now, the reproduction of this map has not come out very well, but I have here a colour print that I'd like to hand out. I think we should give - I'm sure the witness knows this by heart - but give him a copy. Maybe we can put that on the ELMO so that it can be followed. Now, Your Honours this -- this document or this map has been uploaded into e-court as 65 ter number 7175.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, first of all, who prepared this map?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I prepared that map or this map based on the information included in the book "My View of the Break-up," by Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what do the sort of orange arrows illustrate?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the arrows -- I mean, these ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The ones that sort of have a split at the end at the orange?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrows with the split at the end show the access along which according to Kadijevic the JNA was to slice or cut the Croatian territory in order to implement the goals Kadijevic identifies for the first stage of the second phase of the conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what are the -- the red arrows that end with sort of the two lines at the end?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrows you mention now represent the main forces of the JNA which were, according to Kadijevic, planned to carry out offensive operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's important to know. The Bench would like to know when did this happen. What are the dates, please, by and large?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These periods are also given in Kadijevic's book. The first stage of the second phase ranges from end of July 1991 to approximately end of September 1991, according to Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, was this plan actually executed in this form?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. That would bring us to the second stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And before we move to that, I'd like to ask for an exhibit number for this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P244.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And for the discussion of the next phase, I have another map. This is a colour print of the map that Your Honours will find at page 11, or that would be in the B/C/S version page 113 of part 2 of the expert report. That can be placed on the ELMO. This document is 65 ter number 7176.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, who -- who prepared this map?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I prepared this map based on the information I found in the book by Veljko Kadijevic, "My View of the Break-up."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you explain us now what the second phase -- the second stage of the second phase was?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. According to Kadijevic, the second stage of the second phase of the conflict covered the time period from September 1991 until the acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan which corresponds with early 1992. And Kadijevic writes in his book that the initial plan or the initial strategic plan could only be implemented in what he calls considerably modified form; and according to Kadijevic, the only reason for this modification was the lack of response to mobilisation and also what he calls the organised desertion of the JNA reserve corps. So Kadijevic then lists the main tasks for the JNA during what he calls the modified plan, and I will read it out from my report which is a quotation from the book: "In close coordination with the Serb insurgents..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly give us a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- "... all Serb regions in Croatia, except for the part Western Slavonia, were liberated." And this more or less corresponds with one-third of the Croatian territory. Kadijevic adds: "The future army of the Serbian Krajina was built up in the course of the fighting and equipped by the JNA with corresponding arms and material."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And there was a request from the translation booth. This is at page 11 or page 112 of the B/C/S version that this quote came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, so I took the information from Kadijevic's book, and I compared it then with the map that was agreed upon between the two parties when they accepted the Vance Plan, and then I put that information into a map to illustrate what Kadijevic writes in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your report, you have also -- you have also reviewed a number of statements by the accused about where Serb forces should be deployed. In your assessment, do these statements correspond to where forces were actually deployed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement made -- the statements made by Mr. Seselj actually emphasise the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line, which, if I can express myself that way, was much more ambitious than the end result we see at the map here; and, at that stage, Mr. Seselj also expresses his disapproval of the end stage, criticising Kadijevic personally for the failure to achieve the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the accused on your -- did you agree with the aim of protecting Serbs, as it was put, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But I would ask that actually the line we have discussed goes beyond the protection of the Serbs because it covers areas where, at least in 1991, there were no significant -- there was no significant presence of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move in now to the specifics of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, but -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a number for the second map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As Your Honour mentioned, both Kadijevic and Adzic, his deputy, are alleged to have been members of the JCE in this case. There are two exhibits which are discussed in detail in the expert report. They're also in the binder. They are 65 ter number 553 and 569. I think it would be useful if we just take a brief look at that. Maybe we could call up 553 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is a Federal Secretariat for National Defence bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's on page 2, that is in e-court page 3, of the document. In the B/C/S version, it's the first page. Sorry. Yes, it's the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you tell us what this document is and why you have cited it in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The bulletin was created by the information service at the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, or for national defence. It was both -- it was mainly published in English but also in B/C/S, and the publication in English was intended in order to make the information accessible to the international media. This issue of the bulletin includes a statement by General Kadijevic, dated the 3rd of October. So it's a different page than the one that is visible on e-court, at least for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, in the English version, we should move one page further. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Down at the second half of the page, the statement begins.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So statement is dated the 3rd of October, 1991. So it's two days after the establishment of the state of imminent threat of war by the SFRY Presidency, and Kadijevic gives his views of the situation. He starts -- or in the beginning of his statement, he issues -- he provides his opinion on his Supreme Command, which is Stipe Mesic. And, later on, he provides his assessment of what is happening of the -- of the developments in Croatia. I used this document because the choice of terms to characterise the situation is quite remarkable for someone at the level of Kadijevic, and also because this is -- I also include it because it's a contemporaneous document; whereas, the book we have been discussing was only published in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was remarkable -- why do you say quite remarkable for somebody at his level. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he publicly states that he -- I mean, he publicly criticises his Supreme Commander. I think it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could move in e-court in the English version one page on, and I in the B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I'm wrong. It's on the previous page, for the opinion on the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: All right. So could we move, I'm sorry, one page back again. If you could turn to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. In the last paragraph, he asks what kind of Supreme Commander do we have. He also says at the end of the paragraph: "Such an attitude the Supreme Commander and the prime minister towards their own army is not known anywhere else in the world." Now, that is not the most important in the context of my report. Then we go to the next page of the public statement of the federal secretary for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. So if we move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe we are at the middle paragraphs. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is paragraph, I think the fourth, where it starts with: "What is in force in the Republic of Croatia," and then he uses the term "neo-Nazism." He explains the impact of what he considers neo-Nazism on the Serbian population. Then, further on, he says, in the next paragraph, he actually confirms that in his view the JNA, so the army, is -- the goal is to protect the Serbian population from persecution and annihilation and also the goal is to liberate the army personnel and members of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if Your Honours will -- if you have this exhibit now in your binder, if you would move to the next exhibit which is 569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be sure, Mr. Theunens, Kadijevic's criticism against the Supreme Command was made because Kadijevic saw the Supreme Command as selling out Serbian interests in which context? Was it the Vance Plan or what?--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Kadijevic at that moment is criticising Mr. Mesic himself, the Supreme Commander. This is addressed in my report. But, initially, when the term of Mr. Jovic, Borisav Jovic, as the chairman of the SFRY Presidency, has ended, it was up to Mr. Mesic to take over his position. My understanding of the procedures is that the election of Mr. Mesic should have been a routine act; however, Mesic does not obtain the required number of votes. Then the EC intervenes and Mesic is allowed to become and -- or yes, is allowed to become chairman of the Presidency. However, Kadijevic doesn't accept Mesic and doesn't respect Mesic because, in Kadijevic's view, Mesic is actually only pursuing Croatian goals. For example, from the minutes of the SFRY Presidency session in May -- in March 1991, these minutes are not included in the report, but one can see that there is -- that there are confrontations between Mesic and Kadijevic where Kadijevic says the Croats are attacking the JNA; whereas, Mesic says the JNA is supporting the secessionist Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is quite significant. We all agree on this point. This document or this statement was made on the 3rd of October, 1991. I have a question in a respect. Is this a document in favour of maintaining Yugoslavia as a federation, or is it a document in favour of the Serbs? Because if you look at the title of the document, the beginning of the document, you read "Citizens of Yugoslavia," not "Citizens of the Republic of Serbia," and then "Members of the armed forces of Yugoslavia." We could, therefore, think that his logic or his idea is to promote Yugoslavia, to maintain Yugoslavia as it is, and we find that he blames the Croats. He directs very sharp criticism at the Croats. He talks about the Republic of Croatia by accusing it of being neo-Nazi, a neo-Nazi republic. That's quite strong coming from someone who is the federal secretary for the army of Yugoslavia. So he criticises the Presidency as well as Croatia, but we also see that he calls on the international community. That's very clear in this document. We can read it in the document. Based on your research, were sanctions taken against him after this statement, because in no army in the world would the political power tolerate that kind of criticism or statement. Were their sanctions taken against him; and if so, what kind? If not, for what reason? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of any sanctions against Kadijevic. He resigned end of 1991 or early 1992, but the reason for his resignation I'm aware of was his poor health condition. Now, in the report, I also included a statement by Colonel-General Adzic, who was the Chief of the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces, dated the 12th of October, 1991, so it is like nine days after Kadijevic's statement. And his statement, the statement of Adzic, includes the same comments or references towards Croatia. Just to finish my reply, even if it's a request to the citizens of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let the Prosecutor proceed. He'll probably deal with it in the next document, but one more thing. We have a very strongly worded document, a very harsh document. Did you try and find out in the press at the time, in the media at the time, whether this had any impact in the media, any fallout in the media? Did you try to find out whether articles were written about it, whether criticism as levelled at him, whether politicians expressed their support or their criticism following this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not analysed the particular media coverage of this statement, but I would say that it -- it's in the overall spirit of what was published in the newspapers, especially the state-controlled press; and not only newspapers, but also it was said on TV and radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is these -- the kind of language seen here, does that resemble the kind of language in the statements by the accused that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the 12th October statement by Adzic, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is the document that is found at 65 ter number 569 that I was going to take Your Honours to, if we could call it up in e-court. Maybe I can just say, to the court staff, we are out of situations that we need to put under seal. All this can be broadcast. Yeah. I was going to tender these two documents in a bit together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, you -- you refer to this, and we just talked about the use of similar language. If we look at the first page, at the last paragraph in the English version. Mr. Theunens, is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where it says it's rather about defending parts of the Serbian people from genocide, from biological extermination with which they are threatened, by resurrected Fascism in Croatia, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the witness has already explained the relevance of these two documents, and at this point I would like to tender, therefore, 65 ter numbers 553 and 569.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 553 will be Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- will be Exhibit number P247.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll now move to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I don't seem to have this document P554. 553 and 569, I suppose. The interpretation that I got was 554; whereas, I have 553 and 569. So I'm wondering which it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. You have the correct documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, moving now, zooming in, so to speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. You requested the admission of these two documents, 553 and 569, and I see that the registrar has given just one number, P247, but we should have two numbers. One for 553 and one for 569. Because when I look at the transcript, I only see one exhibit number, P247. I don't see P246.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 553 will be Exhibit number P246, and 65 ter number 569 will be Exhibit number P247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. That's very clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise. It was probably me jumping in, speaking over the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, moving now to the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, first what was the strategic significance of this region?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when -- when we look at the map, we see that region borders Serbia. The border is from, in most of the areas, the Danube River. Also, based on the statements of General Panic, who was the commander of the 1st military distinct, Vukovar, the city of Vukovar, which is situated in Eastern Slavonia on the Danube, was of strategic importance both for the Croats and for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in this area --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is mentioning the statement by General Panic here. Now, I have not been provided with that statement, and it was not used in the report. I know for certain that the statement exists because four years ago I came across a short excerpt from the statement. So I should have been supplied with the statement, because my name is mentioned and mention is made of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this statement by Panic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement by Panic is the statement Panic made. It's footnote 240 in part 2 of the report, English page 101. It's the statement he made for BBC, "Death of Yugoslavia", i.e., the transcript of his interview. I quoted, yeah, the statement Panic made when asked about why Vukovar was so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the part is quoted in full -- or the relevant part is quoted in the report at page 101, which is page 219 of the B/C/S version. I believe that the Exhibit number is -- 65 ter 1970. And, as all other exhibits in this case, it has been disclosed to the accused. So there is to basis for this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I want to answer Mr. Seselj. I was looking at the footnote, this footnote 240, because the witness is telling us that this is an interview Panic gave to the BBC. We have the number of the video, V004026; 004026, again. This video should have been disclosed to you, Mr. Seselj. You should have it in your possession because it bears an ERN number. This Panic statement should be amongst all the videos you've been given. Is that correct, Mr. Marcussen? Am I mistaken this has probable been handed over to Mr. Seselj as part of ERN Exhibit 0467824.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. It who is now occurred to me that the accused has systematically refused to accept anything in electronic form, including videos or DVDs. So whether the accused has decided to return this to us or refused to receive it, it might actually have happened; but we have certainly made efforts to provide this to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, the problem is probably that this video was a DVD; and if you had refused that at the time, you never saw it. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problems lies elsewhere, Mr. President. General Zivota Panic, the commander of the 1st Military District whose military group engaged in the liberation of Vukovar, gave a statement to the Hague Tribunal. Now I once had in my possession, four years ago, a small excerpt from that statement, and I wrote to the Trial Chamber and requested in writing that I be given the whole of General Panic's statement which I have not received yet. It is highly relevant for this expert report, and I know what I'm talking about. That programme, "Death of Yugoslavia," whether I received them from them or not, I have it down on paper. I did the transcript myself. But General Panic's statement to the Prosecution is what I need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen. General Panic, I understood who he was. Looking at the exhibit that had been admitted by the Trial Chamber in the framework of questions asked by Mr. Nice and Mr. Milosevic to Mr. Seselj during the Milosevic case, where I quote out of memory, Mr. Seselj was accusing this general of having escaped with millions that he had taken from the Vukovar bank. So you see I know the case well. So, if General Panic was heard by the OTP, you are -- you must absolutely give the statement to Mr. Seselj, because General Panic is involved in Vukovar, and Vukovar is part of the indictment. So first question: Was General Panic heard by the OTP; and, if so, why wasn't this disclosed to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, first of all, the transcript of the testimony in the Milosevic case would have been disclosed to the accused. I am not able to, on the fly here in court, tell you whether or not we have a statement and what the status of disclosure of that is. Well, maybe I actually am, if Your Honours would bear with me for a second. It appears that we don't have a statement, but -- actually, it looks like maybe the witness is aware of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that Mr. Panic was interviewed, but I'm not sure whether he was interviewed as a witness or as a suspect. And if he was interviewed as a suspect, the videotapes are not necessarily transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll look into this and try to get back to you answer on this. I don't think we can fix it right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Check into this, please, because your collaborators seems to tell you that he was heard as a suspect, and it would be good to speak with a single voice within the OTP. But Mr. Seselj seems to know that something occurred, so there is something. So just check during the break, and you'll tell us after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As usual, our expert is right, and we do have a recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information and knowledge, even this witness took part in the interviewing of General Panic, but I'm not quite sure about that. Now, Mr. President, just a slight correction. You just had a very slight correction. It's not General Panic that took millions from the Vukovar bank, but General Vasiljevic, the head of the security service. General Panic died in the meantime, so it wouldn't be a good thing to leave that uncorrected. It's the other one that took the millions, stole the millions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. You're absolutely right. It's the other general who ran off with the money, and General Panic is deceased, passed away. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Within which military district did Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem fall?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem fell within the zone of operations of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you have already testified about the organisation of two Operational Groups, but maybe you could just very quickly remind us how the forces were organised in the area.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the latest, at the end of September 1991, there are two Operational Groups, Operational Group North and Operational Group South, as well as the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Operational Group South is the one that's covering Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the limit or the separation between OG North and OG South was constituted by the Vuka River, which actually runs through Vukovar, which means that, I mean, the largest part of Vukovar is was south of the river. So the area south of Vuka was in zone of responsibilities of OG South, and the area north of the Vuka River, including Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje, was in the zone of responsibility of OG North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned, a couple of times, the Guards Motorised Brigade as a special -- sort of a special unit in the status. What was the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Guards Motorised Brigade was -- was described in JNA literature as an elite unit. It was directly subordinated to the federal secretary for People's Defence, through his Chief of Cabinet at the time, Colonel Vuk Obradovic. The Guards Motorised Brigade had the task to protect the military members of the Supreme Command, and also had ceremonial duties. It was a particularly strong brigade from the point of view of the equipment because it had three motorised battalions. It had one armoured battalion equipped with the most modern tanks at the time within the JNA, the M-84. It had also two military police battalions which was more than any other JNA brigade, and one of these military police battalions had anti-terrorist units. It was also particularly strong from the point of view of manpower, because only the best trained and the best qualified and the manpower of the highest quality was admitted into the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the time for the break has come up, so I think before I continue we should break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. We will now have a break. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Let me tell the Prosecution that you have about an hour and five minutes left. This is what Mr. Registrar told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue with the witness, I thought I should just address first the issue of the interview with General Panic. We have -- we have recordings of interviews. They have not been transcribed. And if the accused would like, we can provide him with a DVD of these interviews. I'm asking the accused to indicate whether he's willing to accept it before I set in motion the recording of these things beyond a DVD, because the usual thing is we get them back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you will recall, at the time you were the Pre-Trial Judge, the problem I had with the Prosecutor providing me with exculpatory material under Rule 68(1). Now, the Prosecution said that it had 270.000 pages in different format, on paper, on disks, on tapes, or whatever. Now, a negligible amount of that material has been disclosed to me or was disclosed to me in the meantime, but you know I can even enter the ranks of the OTP and learn of things that they thought I would never learn. Now, the Prosecutor is here to tell you -- has he only got the tape of the interview or he's got a signed statement by General Panic, because if a person is a suspect, they take both. They record the interview and provide the suspect with a tape. Then a statement is compiled, and the statement is offered to that person to be signed. Now, the Prosecutor is keeping quiet about this. As far as I know, there is a tape of the interview and a statement by the person. And according to your ruling, they have to provide me everything in written form on paper. Now, I don't have time to go into what they have or have not, or what they discussed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen, you weren't there and neither was Mr. Mundis; but during the pre-trial phase, we found out that the accused had been notified by the OTP that there was 270.000 pages of document. I can't remember the figure. That came under Rule 68. When we found this out, the Chamber made a decision, asking Prosecution to take all necessary steps to disclose all these documents, but we also asked Mr. Seselj to provide key words for searches to the Prosecution or to make the work simpler. And, obviously, it seems that the efforts that were undertaken were halted at one point in time. Now, whatever the case, technically if General Panic was heard, I'm sure he must have been heard as a suspect. If he was heard as a suspect, he must have had an interpreter, probably a lawyer, and then there's always a written trace. You don't just have the recording, no just the video ordering, because the document is then sent over and signed. Maybe it wasn't done this in case. It was just an interview, conversation, a videotape, and no written statement. I don't know. Mr. Seselj is telling us something that he's already said in the Milosevic case, that he's got connections at the OTP. He knows what's happening at the OTP. That's what he's saying. He says that he's got hints and clues that led him to believe there is a written statement. Then you're nodding your head saying no. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From the information I have received during the break, there are -- there exist only the recording. There is no written statement. There are instances where the Prosecution do a suspect -- record a suspect interview and a statement. There are also situations where we don't do that. I don't know whether the accused, because he have seen these sort of situations, is thinking that we do this every single time, but we don't. As I said, as far as I've been informed we only have the recordings of the interview; and as I said, if the accused would like to receive this on a DVD, this would be provided to him as soon as we can produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Obviously, there is only a DVD recording. That's it. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there must always exist a document which is signed by the suspect. Don't allow the Prosecutor to mislead you on that score. An interview is conducted, then the OTP makes a summary of that interview. The summary of that interview takes the form of a statement, either by an accused or a potential suspect or witness; and then this is offered up to be signed and each page has to be signed. The witnesses sign every page, so how come a suspect wouldn't need to sign every page? That's impossible. So there must be some reason why they refuse to provide me with that document, and I guarantee that the document exists in writing, on paper. I have seen a part of that document. I saw a paragraph where volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party are mentioned and where my name is mentioned. That document is of such an exculpatory nature that on pain of death the Prosecutor wouldn't provide me with that document, because there's this whole version about Vukovar, although we were in a conflict, and I made the regime to replace him from the chief of the -- the person of chief of the General Staff in 1993. The documents exists about that, and this witness must know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I'm a bit surprised that the OTP would hear witnesses without any written trace, with only a DVD as a trace. But if we have a DVD, what does it mean? It means that after the interview, the witness or suspect will not get a document in his own language telling him what he said. Maybe that's the way the OTP operates. I'm heard so much that I can't be surprised any more. But you must be absolutely sure of the fact. Mr. Marcussen, you must be 100 per cent sure of that fact. You're saying that there was no written statement. That's what your colleagues told you. But just imagine that there was one. Then you could be considered as having lied, and that would be extremely serious. So this is really very important, and we need to be a hundred per cent. You need to check with your colleagues whether that is exactly the truth. Just imagine that out of the blue, you know, we suddenly find this written statement. This would be extremely serious. You're telling us, and I fully understand you, that sometimes there are interviews that did not lead to a written statement, which means that it can be used, and it seems to be the case for General Panic. But then why was he a suspect? Normally, when the person is a suspect, he's got a lawyer, he's got an interpreter. Maybe it was an off-record interview, no lawyer, no nothing. What can you tell me about this please? I think you should really double-check to be a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will indeed double-check, and I'm grateful for the Trial Chamber allowing me time to do that. I think I should clarify one thing. When suspects are interviewed and the interviews are recorded, a number of tapes are done simultaneously. So there exist immediately when the interview is done several copies of the interview. These interviews are put in sealed bags. They are signed by those present during the interview, and the suspect is given a copy. So that's the procedure. It's not that there is no trace, and it's not that the Office of the Prosecutor walk away with a copy in some unorganised fashion. It's a different matter of whether or not these interviews then,-- and of course these recordings, are the record of the interview as provided for in the Rule. In some instances, there are suspects -- they're statements reduced from these interviews as well; but as I say, this is not always the practice. But I will look into, again, whether or not we have any written statements generated from these suspect interviews, and I will return to Your Honours on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please check, double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it the normal practice that the interviews are audiotaped or are they videotaped?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That -- that depends on the circumstances. I believe the Rules require audiotape, but sometimes we do the video as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, Rule 43 states that suspects interviews are recorded. So I would like to refer everybody to Rule 43, sixth paragraph down of this article, which reads as follows: "The contents of the recording is transcribed if the suspect becomes an accused," which means there can be audio recordings without any transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second matter, now that we are in sort of the homework section, yesterday we discussed 65 ter number 1913 and what the source of that document was, and I'm informed that the accused is correct about the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I didn't hear what you just said. There was some interruption. So what document are we talking about, and then I have two remarks to make in that regard as well. Could you tell me what document did you refer to me being correct about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1913. That is the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the title of the document, could you give me the title of the document, because I really can't remember all the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was -- you have it. It's in your binder. Have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The document in its English translation is "Report on recent intelligence on paramilitary organisations within certain Serbian and Montenegrin opposition parties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a minute. We said that if we mentioned the source, this should be mentioned in private session. This was addressed in private session yesterday. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I didn't mention the name --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to mention the name of the source. However, handwritten there, it says the 18th of October, and that source at the time was already retired, Mr. President. It was somebody else who occupied the number one post in the service, not to mention the service or the name. It says the 18th of October, 1993 over there. There was somebody else heading the service at the time; whereas, the previous one was in prison; and after being released, he retired. And as a pensioner, at some point he wrote for the Prosecution and then the Prosecution said that the handwritten date should be the 18th of October. And I guarantee that was written for the purposes of the Prosecution three or four years ago. Let's return to General Panic. Issue an instruction to the Prosecutor, while the Prosecutor is in the courtroom, that his service send him this brief -- these brief minutes signed by all the persons taking part in the interview, to see whether a statement was compiled or not. And one more thing that I'd like to draw your attention to, the -- it was the Prosecution's intention to call General Zivota Panic as a witness in certain trials and he refused that. And in preparation for that, they must have had a statement compiled. So that should be checked out in the OTP as well. Not to have the Prosecutor look for this during the break. His service can provide him with the information within the space of three minutes, not to give them enough time to make a new version and correct the previous one, because that's something they resort to as well. I know that full well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the additional detail provided by Mr. Seselj, seemingly the Prosecution wanted to call Mr. Panic to testify in a number of cases and that this gentleman declined; but if this person were to testify, then automatically there would be a written statement, normally speaking. Mr. Mundis is saying that normally speaking, no, not necessarily. So you have told us that there is no written state. I would like you to check this, and I would like you to tell us after the break that you guarantee that there has been no written state. I can't go and check this out in your office. I can't go and check the archives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to remind you of what I requested first, that straight away they give us this piece of paper that was signed by all those present at the interview, at the questioning. And, secondly, if they don't have a written statement, then by Monday morning they could transcribe the interview with General Panic on paper. Now, can you imagine how many statements they have of the same kind of questioning and interviews that my service has not uncovered? My service has been able to uncover some them but not all of them. So imagine how many such examples exist; and if you take them all together, it might be even more than 270.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please check what you can check. If there is nothing whatsoever, then have the tapes translated, so that the accused is informed about this. According to Rule 68, if Mr. Panic says anything which might exonerate the accused, according to Rule 68, he should be informed about this. Even if this does not exonerate to him, according to Rule 66, this should be disclosed. General Panic is mentioned in the expert report. He's there.
