utterances.text: And prosecutions. Right. You've supplement me there. Now, since you're included in the investigations conducted by The Hague Tribunal, you've also took part in interviewing witnesses for the different trials; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you also took part in questioning suspects in the different proceedings; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But on a -- for the suspect interviews, I was present during a number of suspect interviews, but maybe in one or two of the interviews I asked a question. But the suspect interviews were never led or -- by me, or I never played the major role in a suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not saying you played a major role. All I'm interested in hearing is your confirmation, that you took part in the interviews of witnesses and suspects. Now, what your role was is another matter altogether. I don't want to go into that now. Now, since you say you took part in the interviews and questioning, you took part in preparing and proofing the witnesses as it's called for the trials. Is that how you call it, briefing, proofing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I participated in what is called proofing of a number of witnesses who testified in trials at ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And, in certain cases, you sat in the courtrooms during the testimony of some other military experts. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, and I did that on the explicit request of the senior trial attorney who was in charge of the Prosecution in -- in that particular trial or in those trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And since you were a member of the Prosecution team in certain trials, you took part in decision-making, deciding which witness was to be called or not. It's an evaluation, an estimation of what each witness could contribute. So you stated your views, and then the Prosecutor took the final decision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Like any other team member, I could participate in meetings where, for example, the issue of -- of witnesses to be called was discussed, and my contribution then mainly consisted in providing a factual background or as to the position or the knowledge of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you came to work for the ICTY, you signed a statement saying that you would maintain confidentiality, the confidentiality of the Prosecution and so on. I don't know what the actual name of that document was, the statement was, but you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be really honest with you, this may be I think a convenient express, I probably signed such a thing but I don't remember it exactly. And the reason why I say this, in my previous job experience, I was to sign such a statement every six months, yeah, every six months because of security clearance. Here, I do remember I signed a document when I arrived, which also covered that I would not discuss work-related issues with people who had no need to know, but I only signed that once at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I just meant once. I didn't mean that you signed such a thing every day but I'm satisfied with your answer. Now, you took part in the compiling of certain indictments in the sense that you were consulted with respect to the military aspects of the indictments; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But I would like to emphasise that the military aspects, the factual issues or the factual aspects of the -- of these military aspects, I'm not lawyer and I was never consulted on legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's what I say. You took part in compiling the military sections of the indictments, so you dealt with the military issues. Since the Prosecutors are lawyers, they don't know about military issues. You know the military aspects and issues. So you combined your knowledge to come up with an indictment. Now, you also took part in certain amendments and -- may I finish my question? You took part in preparing some amendments to indictments in certain -- for certain trials; right? After a certain amount of time, the Prosecution concluded that an indictment needed to be changed and then they would include you to work on the amendments to the indictment or consults you, what aspects to include, what others to throw out, and things like that. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no particular recollection of -- of participating in amending an indictment during or -- yeah, during a trial. What I wanted to clarify is that I was asked to provide views on -- on military aspects and on factual background, but the fact that I was asked to provide those views does not necessarily means that my views were also included. It's up to the legal staff, and senior trial attorney in particular, and then of course the Prosecutor, to determine what is included in the indictment, yes or no, and how it is compiled. That is not something I am in control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't say you were in control of it. You took part in the extent to which you can contribute to the work through your knowledge. That was just my question. There's no need for you to answer what I'm not asking you. Now, for quite a long time, you had successful cooperation with one of the Prosecutor, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I hope that at one moment I've worked for three or four senior trial attorneys at the same time, and the impression I have is the cooperation with those senior trial attorneys was also successful or positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Theunens, that your cooperation was always positive and successful and every commendation to you, and I can add some in my own name. There's no need for you to try and back that up. Now, you took part in the compilation of the indictment raised against me in 2001, and Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff consulted you in compiling that indictment, right, against me?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She consulted me like any other member of the -- of the trial team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, not all the others. She consulted you as a military expert. She didn't have any other military expert on the team. So for all military aspects in the indictment against me, she consulted you. Am I right there? Were this any other intelligence analysts or military experts who were consulted?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff consulted or not. She didn't share that with me. I can only reply to the question that, indeed, she consulted me for certain issues, military issues. But whether or not she spoke to her people in order to find out about military aspects, I cannot answer that question. It's only herself who can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to be in a situation to question her about that, but your role is important as far as I'm concerned, Mr. Theunens. Now, Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff consulted you when the indictment against me were expanded when preparations for that were being undertaken, and that was towards the end of 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember the -- the correct sequence of events, I may have been consulted or asked to provide information on, for example, particular locations or particular groups or events. But it is not that she asked me, "Well, Theunens, what shall we include in the indictment?" That's not the situation, and I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You cooperated with her in the matter. She, of course, was always the boss, and you in a way were her subordinate, a member of the team. Now, the details of your conversations is something that nobody can know, and I don't suppose you remember all the details either. You can't remember anything precisely. But as an active member for many years of The Hague Tribunal, I assume you should have known and knew that this international court for the former Yugoslavia is very akin to the international court of Rwanda. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that at one moment in time Ms. Carla Del Ponte was the Prosecutor for the two Tribunals, I mean for the ICTY and the ICTR; and that in Rwanda similar crimes as those dealt with here are being, yeah, put for trial. But I don't have more knowledge or experience with the ICTR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you must be aware that the same people sat in Appeals Chambers in the International Tribunal of the ICTY and the Rwanda Tribunal. If I know that, you have to know it, too.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect for these people, but that's not really a matter what -- that I consider of relevance for me. So I -- I didn't know that. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. But you must be aware that this International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, in it's decisions and judgements, refers very frequently to legal precedents of the ICTR and vice versa. The International Tribunal for Rwanda in its decision and judgements very often refers to the precedent set by this Tribunal, or the jurisprudence ever either tribunal, to be more precise. You must be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mean, it's like for anybody else who reads a judgement. He may see references in the footnotes to decisions by other tribunals or even other courts in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you must be aware that there was a case, Prosecutor versus Akayseu in the ICTR, isn't that right, because the judgement in that case is frequently quoted in the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard of the so-called propaganda trial at the ICTR, but I have not been able actually to read the indictment or the judgement or to further study that matter. I regret that, but it was a matter of time management. I've been fairly busy during the seven -- almost seven years I've been working at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as your -- have been testifying here as an expert in more than one case, in the Milosevic case, in the Martic case, in the Vukovar 3 case, Mrksic, and others to be more precise, you must be aware of the decision of the ICTR in the Akayseu case of the 9th of March, 1998, in which there is a sentence which I find particularly important: "In order to be authorised to testify as an expert, a witness must not only be acknowledged in his own domain but must also be impartial in the given case." Are you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I would like to answer that question. The fact that I work for the Prosecution, in my view, does not influence the contents of my report with the exception, of course, that it was somebody from the Prosecution who asked me to write a report about a certain topic. Now, it's up to the Trial Chamber and the Honourable Judges to decide to what extent I have been able to fulfil that task and to what extent I have been impartial in doing that task. I have explained the methodology I applied, and the avoidance of bias is one of the key matters for an intelligence analyst in order to be able to do his or her job. And that has not only been the case while working at the ICTY but also during my previous experience as an intelligence analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I ask you kindly, Mr. Theunens, to make your replies as brief as possible. I'm not attacking you. I'm just stating certain small facts for you to confirm that you're aware of them or not. You are a very valuable expert here in my view, as if I had called you to testify. Are you aware that the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR confirmed this interpretation of the first instance Trial Chamber in the Akayseu case and in its judgement of the 28th of November, 2007. In the Nahimana, Barayagwiza appeal, it adopted the same standpoint on the fact that an expert has to be impartial in a given case? Just confirm whether you know this, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these particular references, but I know the importance of being impartial obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you for your reply, Mr. Theunens. You are a commander of the Belgian army, which is a rank corresponding to captain 1st class in the Serbian or Yugoslavia army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's maybe a translation issue but I'm not a commander. I'm a commandant because a commander is a higher rank. Now, I am familiar with the rank of captain 1st class in the JNA. But while conducting, for example, these interviews with Defence -- with the military witnesses, I've come to the conclusion that the job an average senior captain or captain 1st class would have in the JNA not necessarily -- or does not necessarily correspond with the tasks commandant or somebody with my rank would have to accomplish or accomplished in -- in the Belgian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted to you. I said commandant. So whoever was listening to me heard me say commandant. I didn't want to disparage your rank. It's between captain and major. It's a captain 1st class in the Serb army, but there is no need to go into this question any further. Your chief in this team is Philip Coo, is he not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is Philip Coo's rank?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, and as I replied to a question by the residing Judge, I believe he's a captain or major, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure; and, obviously, I've not checked with him after I gave the answer during my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he might have a rank similar to yours, one star, more or less. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and it has never been an issue, as far as I know, within the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Theunens, that the OTP engaged Philip Coo as a Prosecution expert witness in the case of Milan Milutinovic and others?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Theunens, that the Trial Chamber in that case, presided over by Judge Bonomy, rejected Philip Coo's expert report on the grounds that the author of the expert report was too close to the Prosecution? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Your Honours, and also of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your opinion, are you too close to the Prosecution, especially bearing in mind that you are doing your very best to avoid telling me and everybody else and the public what your monthly salary is in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Which part is it that the accused would like the witness to respond to? There is a comment in there about the salary. I think we have to be clear about what the witness is being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's no point on belabouring the point on the salary. If you go on the site of the ICC, you will discover that against the employment box you will find salary figures. Everyone has understood that this man is not working for free, and he has to be adequately paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know why the salary should and secret. I remember the first salary I received as a young assistant lecturer in my time. But my question, again, is not what his salary is, but whether he's too close to the OTP to be an expert in this case, bearing in mind the case of Philip Coo in another case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that it's first and foremost a legal question. I wish to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that, even after the decision of the Milutinovic Trial Chamber, I was allowed to testify in the Martic trial -- or I will rephrase that. I testified in the Martic trial prior to the decision. But even when the Martic Defence brought up the Milutinovic Trial Chamber decision in order to have my testimony removed, the answer of the Trial Chamber, the Martic Trial Chamber, was that they were not bound by the decision of another Trial Chamber. The same applies to the Vukovar Trial Chamber. Now, as I mentioned in the beginning of the testimony, this report has only been compiled by me. There was nobody else involved in compiling this document with the exception of people reading the report in order to identify typographical errors. This means it is me, and nobody else, who decided about the contents of this report. Now, again, I think it is a question -- a question of bias or the absence of bias, and that's only something, in my view, the Trial Chamber can decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, next week you will be able to address this issue again, but now we need to adjourn the hearing because we must finish at a quarter to 2.00. Mr. Seselj, I'd like to draw your attention to the document which the Prosecutor has given us relating to the admission of documents. There are several hundreds of documents which are documents which are quoted in the footnotes of the expert report. Some documents have been admitted, some documents are part of the expert report, but some documents have not been discussed during the hearing. So it would be a good thing if you had a look at these documents. You have ample time to do so between today and next week. You will realise that these documents are numbered. These documents have titles. These documents have dates, and there is a reference to the report, to the section of the report it concerns, and footnote numbers are also indicated. So it would be a good idea, once you have finished your cross-examination, to tell us, either orally or perhaps even in writing because orally this might take quite some time, according to you which documents are not a problem and which documents are documents you object to. But you will have to tell us this in detail, because the Trial Chamber at the end of the day will have to rule on the admission or non-admission of these documents. So you will see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've just been handed a document in the English language. I cannot state anything based on this document. I have to have all the titles in Serbian, and then I can tell you what my standpoint is. But I oppose, categorically, the admission of any document not presented in the courtroom and not presented to the witness during examination. I will challenge the admission of the so-called expert report. That's my position, but this list has to be submitted to me in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Trial Chamber has understood that you categorically oppose the admission or the tendering of any document that has not been shown to a witness. But, Mr. Seselj, let me remind you that according to the case law of the Chambers of this Tribunal, which has been corroborated by the Appeals Chamber, authorises the admission of documents, even when these documents have not been shown to the witness, because we have a whole series of documents coming in; and if we have to look at each document one after the other, we would still be here for centuries. So some documents can be admitted without the witness have to confirm that the appointment of such-and-such a person was seen. So we have perfectly understood your objection, but alternatively, let me nonetheless invite you to look at each document in turn to see whether they are of interest to you. Now I'm turning to the Prosecutor. Mr. Seselj would like to have the titles of all these documents in his own language, which I made a mental note of, because I realised that, of course, some of the titles are in his own language but some of the titles are in English. So if Mr. Seselj is not conversant in English, nonetheless he might be able to understand some of the titles. Nevertheless, he is entitled to have all these titles in his own language. So, over the weekend, maybe you could have these titles translated into B/C/S and fax them to him over the weekend. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor submitted a motion that all the documents quoted in the report be admitted into evidence in the expectation that the report itself would be admitted into evidence, but please don't pre-judge the issue because I'm convinced you will not admit the report. I have already presented many arguments why the report should not be admitted, and I tend to present many more. So we don't know yet whether the report will be admitted or not. Why should I deal with documents that have not been mentioned when I expect the report to be rejected? I think it's impossible for this report to be admitted into evidence as an expert report, so why should I deal with documents not mentioned at all? If I find I need a document in my cross-examination, I might bring it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will do what you seem fit, but it was my duty to tell you that the Prosecutor has filed an oral motion, together with a written document, asking for the admission of documents which are mentioned in the expert report, and I understood that you are against the admission of this expert report. You have developed your arguments, and you will continue to do so next week; but at the end of the day, the Trial Chamber will have to determine the matter. Now, for the Trial Chamber to be able to do so and have a good understanding and knowledge of the facts, perhaps you could shed some light on this, and this would be a very good idea. It is now 10 to 2.00. I apologise for having overstepped our time by five minutes. As you know, we shall meet again next week where we'll be sitting in the morning; and on Tuesday, we will be sitting at 8.30 in the morning unless I'm mistaken. The registrar confirms that we will be sitting at 8.30 on Tuesday. We shall meet again then. In the meantime, Witness, I ask you to have no contacts whatsoever with the OTP. Thank you, and see you on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of February, 2008, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
